questions.question: When forces on an object are balanced, the object will:

choices.C: Move at constant velocity or stay at rest

questions.explanation: Balanced forces mean the net force is zero. With no net force, there is no acceleration, so the object either stays at rest or continues at constant velocity (Newton's First Law).
steps: Without acceleration, velocity does not change
Therefore motion stays constant or remains at rest
questions.fastStrategy: Net force zero? Expect no acceleration—motion stays the same.

questions.question: A runner moves at 15 m/s for 4 seconds. How far does the runner travel?
questions.explanation: Distance = speed × time. Multiply 15 m/s by 4 s to get 60 meters.
steps: Plug in v = 15 m/s and t = 4 s
questions.fastStrategy: Constant speed problems: distance = speed × time.

questions.question: The SI unit of work is the:
questions.explanation: Work is measured in Joules (J). One Joule equals one Newton-meter (force × distance). Newton is force, Watt is power, Pascal is pressure.
steps: Recall work formula: W = F × d
SI unit for work is Joule
Newton = force, Watt = power, Pascal = pressure
questions.fastStrategy: Work uses Joules; think Newton-meter.

questions.question: Which object has greater inertia?
questions.explanation: Inertia is resistance to changes in motion and is directly related to mass. A 10 kg toolbox has more mass and therefore more inertia than a 1 kg book.
questions.fastStrategy: More mass = more inertia.

questions.question: If the net force on an object doubles while its mass stays the same, its acceleration:
questions.explanation: From F = ma, acceleration is proportional to net force when mass is constant. Doubling net force doubles acceleration.
steps: If F doubles, a must double to keep equality
questions.fastStrategy: With constant mass, acceleration scales directly with net force.

questions.question: A rocket moves forward because the exhaust gases push backward. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Exhaust gases pushed backward provide an opposite push that propels the rocket forward.
steps: Identify paired forces: gas backward, rocket forward
First Law is inertia; Second is F = ma
questions.fastStrategy: Action-reaction pairs signal Newton's Third Law.

questions.question: On Earth, the acceleration due to gravity is approximately:
questions.explanation: Standard gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface is about 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10 m/s² for quick calculations).
steps: 4.9 is roughly half, often used in equations for distance
20 is too high, 1 is too low
questions.fastStrategy: Use g ≈ 10 m/s² for quick math; exact is 9.8.

questions.question: At the top of its path, a ball thrown straight up has:
questions.explanation: At the highest point, the ball's velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts downward at about 9.8 m/s², so acceleration is downward.
steps: Recognize velocity is momentarily zero at the top
Acceleration is not zero or upward
Choose zero velocity with downward acceleration
questions.fastStrategy: Peak of a throw: v = 0, a = g downward.

questions.question: Which frictional force is typically greatest when starting to move a heavy box?
questions.explanation: Static friction (before motion) is usually greater than kinetic friction (during motion). More force is needed to start moving an object than to keep it sliding.
steps: Recall static friction resists start of motion
Static friction coefficient is usually higher than kinetic
questions.fastStrategy: It’s hardest to start moving—static friction is highest.

questions.question: If you push a box with 20 N while friction also equals 20 N in the opposite direction, the box will:

choices.C: Move at constant speed or stay still

questions.explanation: Net force is zero (20 N forward and 20 N backward). With no net force, there is no acceleration; motion stays the same (rest or constant speed).
steps: Object remains at rest or continues constant speed
questions.fastStrategy: Equal opposite forces cancel; expect no acceleration.

questions.question: Using a longer ramp to load a crate reduces the effort because:

choices.A: Gravity is weaker on a ramp
choices.B: The mass of the crate decreases
choices.C: The force is applied over a longer distance

questions.explanation: An inclined plane trades distance for force. Pushing over a longer distance requires less force to raise the same height (work stays the same).
steps: For the same work, required force decreases
Gravity and mass stay the same
questions.fastStrategy: Long ramp: less force, more distance.

questions.question: A bike speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time. (20 m/s - 0) ÷ 5 s = 4 m/s².
questions.fastStrategy: Acceleration = change in speed divided by time.

questions.question: Applying a 12 N net force to a 3 kg cart produces what acceleration?
questions.explanation: From F = ma, a = F/m. Here a = 12 N ÷ 3 kg = 4 m/s².
questions.fastStrategy: Divide net force by mass to get acceleration.

questions.question: The same force is applied to a 1 kg object and a 10 kg object. Which accelerates more?
questions.explanation: With F = ma, for the same force, smaller mass results in larger acceleration. The 1 kg object accelerates more than the 10 kg object.
steps: a = F/m ⇒ larger m gives smaller a
1 kg has smaller mass than 10 kg
questions.fastStrategy: Same force: lighter object accelerates more.

questions.question: At the top of a roller coaster hill (ignoring friction), most of the coaster's mechanical energy is:
questions.explanation: At the highest point, speed is lowest and height is greatest, so most mechanical energy is gravitational potential energy. As it descends, that potential converts to kinetic.
steps: Identify energy forms: potential depends on height
Top of hill = maximum height, minimal speed
Thus energy stored as gravitational potential
Kinetic increases as the coaster goes down
questions.fastStrategy: High position = high potential energy; speed grows as it falls.

questions.question: If an object's speed increases by the same amount each second, the object has:
questions.explanation: A steady change in speed per unit time means acceleration is constant (uniform acceleration).
steps: Acceleration is rate of change of velocity
Same change every second ⇒ rate is constant
questions.fastStrategy: Equal speed change each second = constant acceleration.

questions.question: How much work is done if a force is applied but the object does not move?
questions.explanation: Work requires displacement. If there is no movement (distance = 0), work done is zero regardless of the applied force.
steps: Force alone without motion does no work
questions.fastStrategy: No motion means no work done.

questions.question: A fixed pulley mainly helps by:
questions.explanation: A fixed pulley lets you pull down to lift up, changing the direction of the applied force. It does not reduce mass or create energy.
steps: It redirects force but provides no mechanical advantage in ideal case
questions.fastStrategy: Fixed pulley = direction change, not force multiplication.

questions.question: Momentum always points in the same direction as an object's:
questions.explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity (p = mv). It is a vector with the same direction as velocity.
steps: Mass and weight have no direction component
questions.fastStrategy: Momentum vector aligns with velocity.

questions.question: A car turns left at a constant speed. Is it accelerating?

choices.D: Only if it also speeds up

questions.explanation: Acceleration is any change in velocity, including direction. Turning left changes velocity direction, so the car is accelerating (centripetal acceleration).
questions.fastStrategy: Direction change alone counts as acceleration.

questions.question: If 100 J of work is done in 10 seconds, the power output is:
questions.explanation: Power equals work divided by time. 100 joules over 10 seconds is 10 watts (100 ÷ 10).
questions.fastStrategy: Divide work by time to get Watts.

questions.question: If a force acts opposite an object's motion, the object will:
questions.explanation: A force opposite the direction of motion provides negative acceleration, reducing the object's speed.
steps: Identify force direction is opposite motion
questions.fastStrategy: Force opposite velocity = deceleration.

questions.question: What does the slope of a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.explanation: The slope (change in velocity over time) on a velocity-time graph equals acceleration.
steps: Slope = change in vertical / change in horizontal
Vertical axis is velocity, horizontal is time
questions.fastStrategy: On v–t graphs, slope is acceleration.

questions.question: If both mass and acceleration double, the net force required becomes:
questions.explanation: From F = ma, doubling mass (2m) and acceleration (2a) gives F = (2m)(2a) = 4ma, four times the original force.
steps: Therefore force is four times larger
questions.fastStrategy: F = ma scales with both factors; doubling both ⇒ 4× force.

questions.question: According to the work-energy idea, net work done on an object equals its change in:
questions.explanation: The work-energy theorem states that net work on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. Potential energy changes involve height but net work relates directly to kinetic energy change.
steps: Momentum and mass are not equal to work directly
questions.fastStrategy: Net work changes kinetic energy (ΔKE).
